walkthroughs.body_html:
Medieval doctors blamed illness on the four humours, God, or bad air called miasma.

Treatments included bleeding, purging and prayer. The Church protected Galen's ideas and banned dissection. Hospitals were run by monks and nuns who offered care, not cures.

In 1348 bubonic plague reached England. People thought God or miasma caused it.

They tried flagellation, herbs and lucky charms. About one third of the population died. Towns later passed quarantine rules — an early sign of public health thinking.

Printing and dissection let doctors check Galen for themselves.

Vesalius published The Fabric of the Human Body in 1543, correcting Galen's anatomy. In 1628 William Harvey proved the heart pumps blood round the body in a closed circuit.

mcqs.q: Why was Vesalius significant in the history of medicine?
options: Vesalius discovered the cause of disease and ended humoral theory.
The four humours were invented by Pasteur to explain bacteria.
Vesalius invented the microscope.
His 1543 De Humani Corporis Fabrica corrected Galen's errors via human dissection and accurate illustration, founding modern anatomy though not curing disease.

mcqs.q: What was the theory of the four humours?
options: Disease was caused by imbalance of blood, phlegm, yellow bile and black bile; treatment aimed to rebalance them via bloodletting, purging or diet. It dominated for nearly 2,000 years.
Medieval doctors knew about germs but used humours because they had no medicine.
The four humours were invented by Pasteur to explain bacteria.
Vesalius invented the microscope.

mcqs.q: What did Magna Carta actually do in 1215?
options: The four humours were invented by Pasteur to explain bacteria.
It was a peace treaty between King John and rebel barons protecting baronial privileges and limiting arbitrary royal taxation and imprisonment — it was annulled within months.
Magna Carta abolished the monarchy and created Parliament.
Magna Carta gave ordinary English people democratic rights and freedom.
